title: The Room Above the Weir
passages:
The stair ended and she was in a round room with no door behind her, her coat still dripping from a rain she could not remember standing in. A clock the size of a cartwheel hung above the desk, its minute hand trembling. On the desk lay a book, open, its spine stamped *Auto*, and every page she turned was blank. Beside it a slate, in a hand not hers: *Read the last page. Write one thing true. Leave a note. You have less time than you think.*

She read the last page twice. It was blank as all the others, and the blankness felt less like absence than like a held breath. She reached for the men who must have come before her and found no faces, no yesterday at all — only the wet coat, the cold hands, the pen already warm between her fingers.

So she began. She wrote: *In the town of Harrow there is a bell that rings once for every person the water takes.* She wrote it slowly, to give her fear something to do, and when she lifted the pen the window at her shoulder had stopped being dark.

Below, where there had been nothing, there were lamps: one, then four, then a street's worth, burning down toward a river. Roofs came up out of the ground like breath on cold glass. A tower assembled itself course by course, and in it a bell she had never seen swung and struck once, and she felt the note in her teeth.

The minute hand jumped. Her fingers had begun to feel borrowed. She wrote fast on the slate: *It works. I wrote a bell and the town has one. Do not write anything you are not willing to meet.* Then the clock struck, the room folded like a page, and the last thing she did was turn to the next leaf.
